newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. cites worst violence in Cyprus since 1974.
newsitem.headline: U.N. cites worst violence in Cyprus since 1974.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said on Tuesday the situation on the divided island of Cyprus had deteriorated in the last six months, accompanied by violence not seen since 1974.

That was the year troops from Turkey landed in northern Cyprus after a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece, resulting in the virtual partition of the island between Greek and Turkish Cypriots.

"The situation in Cyprus deteriorated in the last six months. There was violence along the ceasefire lines, including the unnecessary and disproportionate use of lethal force by the Turkish/Turkish Cypriot side, to an extent not seen since 1974," Boutros-Ghali said in a written report to the Security Council.
"The atmosphere between the two communities was marked by increasing distrust and hostility," he added.

Two Greek Cypriots were killed by Turks and Turkish Cypriot civilians during a buffer zone protest in August, he said. In September, a Turkish Cypriot sentry was shot and killed, and in October a Greek Cypriot was shot and killed after straying into Turkish-held territory.

"Once again I must express serious concern about the excessive levels of military forces and armaments in Cyprus and the rate at which they are being expanded, upgraded and modernised. This can only increase tension on the island and in the region," Boutros-Ghali said.

He recommended another six-month renewal, until June 30, 1997, of the U.N. Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP). Stationed on the island since 1964 following the eruption of inter-communal violence, UNFICYP now comprises 1,162 troops from seven countries and 35 civilian police and is commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahti Vartiainen of Finland.
The United Nations has been trying for decades, without success, to reunite the island under a federal system.

Boutros-Ghali said there had been no significant change in the level of forces and armaments on the Turkish side, which maintained a strength of some 30,000 Turkish and 4,500 Turkish Cypriot troops. On the government side, the National Guard acquired 27 modern T-80UM and 52 AMX-30 main battle tanks, for a total of 123 main battle tanks, while the National Guard's strength stood at about 11,500.

The secretary-general said there had been no progress on the question of reciprocal measures to prohibit live ammunition or weapons, other than hand-held weapons, along the ceasefire lines. There was also no progress on extending a 1989 agreement to abandon some posts on either side.
"There is an urgent need now for leaders on both sides to make a serious effort to reverse the negative trend of recent months and to lead their communities in a more positive direction," he said.

"In word and deed, efforts must be made to build trust and goodwill between the two sides," he said, adding that early agreement on a package of measures to reduce tension along the ceasefire lines would be a significant step forward.
